scenes.heading: Electron configuration and periodic trends
scenes.sub: Where electrons sit decides how an element behaves
scenes.say: Why is sodium so reactive, and why is fluorine so good at grabbing electrons? It all comes down to how electrons are arranged around the nucleus.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Passengers fill the seats nearest the door first
scenes.science: Electrons fill the lowest-energy subshells first
scenes.breaks: electrons don't sit in fixed seats, and 4s fills before 3d, so the order isn't simply shell 1, 2, 3.
scenes.say: Think of passengers getting on an empty bus. They take the seats nearest the door first, just like electrons fill the lowest-energy subshells first. Each double seat is an orbital that holds two at most, and people sit alone before sharing, just like electrons.

scenes.heading: Subshells
points: s, p, d, f hold 2, 6, 10 and 14 electrons
Each orbital holds at most 2 electrons
scenes.say: Shells split into subshells called s, p, d and f, which hold two, six, ten and fourteen electrons. They fill in order, but watch out: four s fills before three d.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Write the electron configurations of calcium (Z = 20) and Ca²⁺.
scenes.say: Calcium has twenty electrons. Fill in order: one s two, two s two, two p six, three s two, three p six, four s two. The calcium two plus ion loses its two four s electrons, so it matches argon.
scenes.caption: Calcium has 20 electrons. Fill in order: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s². Ca²⁺ loses its two 4s electrons, so it matches argon.

scenes.heading: Two exceptions
points: Ions of transition metals lose 4s first
scenes.say: Two exceptions. Chromium ends three d five, four s one, and copper ends three d ten, four s one, because half-full or full d subshells are more stable. And transition metal ions lose their four s electrons first.
scenes.caption: Two exceptions. Chromium ends 3d⁵ 4s¹, and copper ends 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, because half-full or full d subshells are more stable. And transition metal ions lose their 4s electrons first.

scenes.heading: Core charge
scenes.say: Core charge is the net pull on the outer electrons: protons minus inner-shell electrons. Sodium is eleven minus ten, plus one. Chlorine is seventeen minus ten, plus seven. It rises across a period and stays the same down a group.

scenes.heading: The two levers
scenes.say: Two levers explain every trend: core charge and number of shells. Across a period, core charge rises, so atoms shrink and electrons are harder to remove. Down a group, extra shells make atoms bigger and electrons easier to remove.

points: s, p, d, f hold 2, 6, 10, 14 electrons
4s fills before 3d; Cr and Cu are exceptions
Trends: core charge and number of shells
scenes.say: Quick recap. Subshells hold two, six, ten and fourteen electrons. Four s fills before three d, and chromium and copper are exceptions. Core charge is protons minus inner electrons. Every trend comes from core charge and the number of shells. Now try the practice questions!
